TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- For years Ahmad has been unable to find true love. So the 27 year-old bachelor who lives in Tehran is turning to a professional matchmaker. Jafar Ardabili's matchmaking service provides one option for Iranian singles. "I'm searching for a love that lasts," Ahmad said. What's unusual is Ahmad's matchmaker wears a turban, a robe and could be the first-ever Iranian cleric who plays cupid. "First they say 'wow'," Jafar Ardabili said, "then they take a closer look and say 'since he's a cleric we have faith in him.'" Ardabili made his first love match 10 years ago while he taught at a Tehran university. One of his students had a crush on a person, so Ardabili arranged for the two to meet. A few months later they married. The set-up worked so well that Ardabili and his wife opened the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, a service that matched Iranian singles in a supervised setting. In Iran, Islamic law restricts social interaction. "You can't just go after someone in public and say would you like to live with me?" Ardabili said. "Especially the women, who often don't have any right to choose their companion, but in our institute women do have the right to choose." Ahmad would love nothing more than one of those women to choose him. On a Thursday morning he anxiously sat in the institute's waiting room. Ardabili had arranged for Ahmad to meet a young lady. Could she be the one? Ahmad had paid a $100 fee, submitted a picture and his information. In return he has access to thousands of other applicants. Once applicants approve of one another's pictures and profiles Ardabili arranges up to two meetings inside his office. After each meeting, the applicants report back to Ardabili. "When there's no connection they look like wrinkled potatoes," Ardabili said. And when cupid's arrow hits the mark? "They look very eager. They're as happy as an ice cream cone."  Watch Ardabili describe how his service works » . The third meeting for couples takes place outside the institute without supervision. If all goes well, Ardabili arranges for the families to meet and then the couple ties the knot. "You feel good because you're serving humanity," Ardabili said. Ardabili said that during the past 10 years his institute has had more than 50,000 applicants. More than 2,000 of his couples have married without a single divorce, he said. Ardabili gave credit to his 10-member staff that offers counseling to married couples, even sex therapy. "We want to reduce divorce, give families a strong foundation," Ardabili said. On his Web site, Tehran's matchmaking mullah has posted wedding pictures of some of his success stories. Ahmad can't wait to see his picture among them. "At this very moment I'm counting down the days."

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) — Ahmad, a 27-year-old unmarried man from Tehran, has spent years looking unsuccessfully for lasting romance. Now he is seeking help from a professional matchmaker.

One place available to single Iranians is the matchmaking agency run by Jafar Ardabili.

“I’m looking for a love that endures,” Ahmad said.

What makes Ahmad’s situation striking is that the man trying to find him a partner is dressed in a turban and clerical robe — and may be Iran’s first cleric to act as a matchmaker.

“At first people say, ‘Wow,’” Ardabili said. “Then they think about it more and say, ‘Because he is a cleric, we trust him.’”

Ardabili arranged his first romantic pairing a decade ago, when he was teaching at a university in Tehran. One of his students was interested in someone, and Ardabili helped organize a meeting between them. Within a few months, the two were married.

The success of that introduction led Ardabili and his wife to establish the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, where Iranian singles can meet one another in a monitored environment.

In Iran, social contact is limited by Islamic law.

“You cannot simply approach someone in public and ask, ‘Would you like to live with me?’” Ardabili said. “This is particularly true for women, who often do not have the freedom to choose their partner. But at our institute, women do have that choice.”

Ahmad is hoping that one of those women will choose him. On a Thursday morning, he waited nervously in the institute’s reception area. Ardabili had scheduled a meeting for him with a young woman. Ahmad wondered whether she might be the right person.

He had paid a $100 fee, provided a photograph and submitted personal details. In exchange, he gained access to thousands of other people who had applied to the service.

When two applicants approve each other’s photos and profiles, Ardabili sets up as many as two meetings in his office. After every meeting, each person reports back to him.

“If there is no spark, they look like shriveled potatoes,” Ardabili said.

And when the match succeeds?

“They seem very excited. They are as happy as an ice cream cone.”

The couple’s third meeting happens outside the institute and is not supervised. If things continue positively, Ardabili then arranges for the families to meet. After that, the couple gets married.

“You feel good because you are helping humanity,” Ardabili said.

According to Ardabili, more than 50,000 people have applied to his institute over the past decade. He said that more than 2,000 couples matched through the service have married, and that none have divorced.

He credited his 10-person staff, which provides counseling for married couples, including sex therapy.

“Our goal is to lower the divorce rate and help families begin on solid ground,” Ardabili said.

On his website, Tehran’s matchmaking mullah displays wedding photographs from some of the couples he has successfully brought together.

Ahmad hopes his own photo will soon be added to that collection.

“Right now, I’m counting the days,” he said.

counterfactuals.output:
**Tehran cleric turns matchmaking into a mission for Iran’s singles**

**Tehran, Iran** — In a modest office tucked behind a busy street in Tehran, a cleric in a white turban flips through handwritten forms, each one listing hopes, habits and expectations: education level, family background, religious observance — and what kind of spouse the applicant is looking for.

For Jafar Ardabili, the work is not merely administrative. It is, he says, a social and religious duty.

“Marriage is not just a private matter,” Ardabili said. “It strengthens families and protects society. Many young people want to marry, but they do not know where to begin.”

Ardabili runs a matchmaking service aimed at helping single Iranians meet potential spouses in a society where dating can be complicated by tradition, family expectations and economic pressure. Applicants are interviewed, their preferences are recorded, and introductions are arranged with an emphasis on compatibility and family approval.

Among those seeking help is Ahmad, a 27-year-old bachelor from Tehran who says meeting someone through ordinary social circles has become increasingly difficult.

“I have a job, I am ready for marriage, but it is not easy to find the right person,” Ahmad said. “Families have expectations, and young people are under pressure. I came here because I wanted a serious and respectful way to be introduced.”

Iran has long encouraged marriage, but many young people are delaying it because of high living costs, unemployment concerns and the rising expense of housing and wedding ceremonies. For some, traditional matchmaking — often handled by relatives or neighbors — has given way to more organized services, including religiously guided programs like Ardabili’s.

The cleric says his service is not about forcing choices, but about creating an acceptable path for people who want marriage and do not want to rely on chance encounters.

“We listen to both sides,” Ardabili said. “If their values and goals are close, we make an introduction. After that, it is up to the families and the couple to decide.”

Ahmad said he welcomes that structure, even if the process feels formal.

“It is different from meeting someone online or through friends,” he said. “Here, from the beginning, everyone knows the purpose is marriage. That makes things clearer.”

Still, the approach is not without challenges. Young Iranians often balance religious and cultural expectations with changing ideas about relationships, independence and personal choice. Ardabili acknowledges that compatibility is about more than ticking boxes on a form.

“A good marriage needs understanding,” he said. “Faith matters, but kindness, patience and responsibility matter too.”

For Ahmad, the hope is simple: to find someone with whom he can build a stable future.

“I don’t expect perfection,” he said. “I just want someone who shares my values and wants to walk the same path.”

counterfactuals.output:
**In Iran, a Matchmaking Mullah Offers a Traditional Path to Modern Love**

QOM, Iran — On a quiet afternoon in a modest office near one of this city’s busy religious schools, a turbaned cleric sits behind a wooden desk with a notebook, a ringing mobile phone and a small tray of tea. Couples do not come here to confess their sins or seek a legal ruling. They come hoping to get married.

Hojatoleslam Reza Mahmoudi, a middle-aged mullah with a neatly trimmed beard and a soft voice, has become an unlikely matchmaker for young Iranians struggling to find a spouse in a society where old customs and modern expectations often collide.

“I am not here to force anyone,” Mahmoudi says, adjusting his white turban as he flips through a folder of handwritten notes. “My job is to introduce families and create a safe, respectful space for people to talk.”

The meetings he arranges are carefully supervised. A young man and woman may sit across from one another in a small reception room, usually with a female assistant or family members nearby. They discuss education, work, finances, religion, whether they want children and how they imagine married life. If both sides are interested, their families meet. If not, the cleric quietly closes the file and wishes them well.

In Iran, where many marriages are still influenced by family networks, matchmaking is not new. What is unusual is the role Mahmoudi has carved out for himself: part counselor, part community elder, part practical organizer for a generation whose social lives have been transformed by universities, smartphones and economic uncertainty.

“Before, your aunt or neighbor knew someone,” says Fatemeh, 29, a teacher who asked that her last name not be used. “Now people live in apartments, work long hours, and families don’t always know whom to trust. Here, at least, someone has checked the basics.”

Mahmoudi says his process begins with interviews. Applicants fill out forms listing their age, education, occupation, family background and expectations. He asks about temperament and values. He also asks what they can compromise on.

“That is where we learn the most,” he says with a smile. “Everyone has a list. Marriage begins when the list becomes a conversation.”

For some, the appeal is the supervision itself. The meetings allow men and women to speak directly while still respecting conservative social norms. Parents who might be uneasy about casual dating often feel more comfortable when an intermediary is involved.

On a recent day, a 32-year-old engineer arrived with his mother, both visibly nervous. Minutes later, a young woman studying pharmacy entered with her older sister. Tea was poured. Mahmoudi began gently.

“Please don’t give speeches,” he told them. “Speak honestly. Ask what matters.”

At first, the conversation was stiff. Then the woman asked whether the engineer expected his wife to stop working after marriage. He replied that he did not, but wanted to discuss how household responsibilities would be shared. Her sister nodded. Mahmoudi said nothing, taking notes.

Not every meeting succeeds. Some end after 20 minutes. Others continue through several family visits before falling apart over dowry expectations, housing costs or disagreements about where the couple would live. Iran’s economic pressures, especially housing and employment, weigh heavily on marriage decisions.

“Young people want marriage, but they are afraid,” Mahmoudi says. “They ask: Can we afford rent? Can we build a life? Love is important, but so is bread.”

His small operation depends mostly on word of mouth. Some families hear about him at the mosque; others find him through friends or messaging apps. He says he charges little or nothing, though families sometimes make donations to cover office expenses.

Mahmoudi insists he is not running a marriage factory. He rejects the idea that compatibility can be reduced to a form or a pious recommendation. In recent years, he says, he has learned to listen more carefully to women, who are increasingly educated and clear about their expectations.

“A girl may say, ‘I want respect, I want to continue my studies, I want a husband who speaks with me, not at me,’” he says. “These are not unreasonable things.”

One couple, Ali and Zahra, credit Mahmoudi with helping them find each other after several failed introductions. Their first meeting, they recall, was awkward but practical. They talked about faith, careers and whether they preferred living near parents or independently.

“There was no dramatic romance,” Zahra says, laughing. “But there was calm. I felt I could ask questions.”

They married eight months later. Now, when they visit Mahmoudi with their infant son, the cleric beams like a proud uncle.

Still, the work brings criticism. Some younger Iranians view clerical matchmaking as outdated, while some conservatives worry that even supervised meetings give young people too much freedom. Mahmoudi says he hears both sides and tries to stand in the middle.

“If they do not meet and speak, how can they choose?” he asks. “And if there is no trust, how can families feel safe?”

As evening prayers approach, Mahmoudi’s phone buzzes again. A mother is calling about her daughter, a university graduate in Tehran. A father wants to know if there is a suitable match for his son, who has recently returned from military service. Mahmoudi writes down the details, asks a few questions and promises nothing.

“Marriage is not in my hands,” he says. “I only open a door.”

In a country where the path to marriage can be crowded with tradition, aspiration and anxiety, that open door is enough to keep people knocking.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a detailed wire-service report on Tehran’s Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, founded by cleric Jafar Ardabili and his wife, explaining how the matchmaking process works and its success rate.
counterfactuals.output:
**TEHRAN —** In a modest office in the Iranian capital, the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute offers a highly structured answer to one of the most sensitive questions facing many young Iranians: how to find a spouse in a society where traditional family introductions have weakened, but Western-style dating remains socially and religiously controversial.

Founded by cleric **Jafar Ardabili** and his wife, the institute presents itself as a bridge between old and new — a matchmaking service rooted in Islamic values, family involvement and psychological screening, but organized with files, interviews and a managed database of candidates.

Ardabili, a Shiite cleric, says the institute was created to help young people marry more easily and responsibly at a time when economic strain, urban life and shifting social habits have made marriage more difficult. His wife plays a central role in the operation, particularly in interviewing women and working with families.

### How the process works

The Amin Institute does not operate like a dating agency in the Western sense. Men and women do not browse photos or contact one another directly. Instead, the process is mediated by staff, counselors and families.

Applicants begin by registering with the institute and completing detailed forms. These typically cover:

- age, education and occupation  
- family background  
- religious observance  
- expectations about marriage  
- views on work, children and household roles  
- economic circumstances  
- personality traits and preferences for a spouse  

After registration, applicants are interviewed by institute staff. The interviews are intended to assess seriousness, compatibility, family expectations and potential areas of conflict. In keeping with conservative social norms, male and female applicants are usually handled separately, with women often interviewed by female staff.

The institute then searches its records for possible matches. Compatibility is judged not only by age and education, but also by religious outlook, cultural background, family status and expectations about married life.

If staff identify a potential match, the families are usually contacted first. Only after both sides express interest does the process move forward to a supervised introduction. Meetings may take place at the institute or in a family setting, with relatives involved from the beginning.

The couple can then meet and speak within boundaries acceptable to their families and the institute. If the two sides remain interested, the families continue discussions over practical matters such as finances, housing, employment and wedding arrangements.

The institute also offers counseling and guidance before marriage, emphasizing communication, religious duties, conflict resolution and realistic expectations. Ardabili has said the goal is not simply to arrange weddings, but to reduce the likelihood of divorce by screening couples carefully before engagement.

### A modern response to a social problem

Iranian officials and religious leaders have long expressed concern about delayed marriage, rising divorce rates and the economic pressures facing young adults. Housing costs, unemployment and inflation have made marriage increasingly difficult for many families.

At the same time, traditional matchmaking through relatives and neighbors has become less reliable in large cities such as Tehran, where families may live far from extended kin networks. Institutes such as Amin have emerged to formalize a role once played informally by relatives, community elders and religious figures.

The Amin Institute says it tries to preserve family participation while giving young people more choice than a purely arranged marriage. Applicants can reject proposed matches, and no marriage is supposed to proceed without the consent of both parties.

### Reported success rate

The institute claims a high success rate for the marriages it helps arrange. According to figures cited by the institute, a large share of its introductions that lead to marriage remain intact, with a divorce rate far below the national average. Ardabili and his staff attribute that outcome to careful screening, family involvement and premarital counseling.

Those figures, however, are based on the institute’s own tracking and are difficult to verify independently. Success is generally measured by whether a marriage continues after the wedding, rather than by broader measures of marital satisfaction.

Still, supporters say the model offers a practical service in a society where many young people want to marry but lack trusted channels for meeting suitable partners. Critics argue that such systems can reinforce social pressure to marry and may give families too much influence over personal choices.

For Ardabili and his wife, the institute’s mission is straightforward: to make marriage easier while keeping it within religious and cultural boundaries.

“We are not here to create temporary relationships,” the institute’s approach suggests. “We are here to help families build permanent ones.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a CNN transcript-style feature beginning “TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) --” about Ahmad, a lonely bachelor using a cleric’s professional matchmaking service to find lasting love under Iran’s social restrictions.
counterfactuals.output:
TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- In a quiet office tucked behind a busy street in the Iranian capital, Ahmad sits across from a cleric and tries to explain the kind of wife he hopes to meet.

He is in his late 30s, soft-spoken and neatly dressed. He has a steady job, a small apartment and, by his own account, a life that looks stable from the outside. But when he returns home at night, he says, the silence feels heavier than it used to.

“I don’t want a temporary feeling,” Ahmad says. “I want someone to build a life with.”

In Iran, where social life is shaped by religious expectations, family scrutiny and strict rules governing relationships between men and women, finding a partner can be complicated — especially for people who have moved beyond the age when relatives and neighbors typically make introductions.

So Ahmad has turned to an unusual kind of matchmaker: a cleric offering a professional marriage introduction service.

The office does not look like a place for romance. There are no candlelit tables, no music, no casual flirting. Instead, there are forms, interviews and careful questions about faith, income, education, family background and expectations for married life.

The cleric, who says his service is intended to help people marry in a “proper and lasting” way, describes himself less as a matchmaker than as a mediator.

“Young people want marriage, but many do not know how to find the right person,” he says. “Families worry. Society has limits. We try to make the path clear.”

For clients like Ahmad, the appeal is not only religious approval but structure. In a society where dating can be socially risky and public relationships may attract attention, formal matchmaking offers a sanctioned route to courtship.

The process begins with an interview. Ahmad is asked what matters most to him: piety, education, temperament, financial expectations, willingness to live with or near relatives, views on children.

He pauses before answering.

“Kindness,” he says finally. “I can accept many differences if there is kindness and respect.”

The cleric nods and writes it down.

Iran’s marriage culture has been changing for years. Many young Iranians are marrying later, citing economic pressure, housing costs, unemployment and shifting expectations. At the same time, traditional avenues for finding a spouse — extended family networks, neighborhood introductions and community gatherings — have weakened, especially in large cities like Tehran.

That has created space for new forms of matchmaking, from online platforms to religiously supervised services. Some are modern and discreet; others emphasize Islamic values and family involvement. The common promise is the same: a way to meet someone serious about marriage without violating social norms.

Ahmad says he has tried relying on relatives before. The introductions were awkward and often brief. In one case, he says, the families disagreed before he and the woman had spoken more than twice. In another, expectations about money ended the conversation early.

“People think if a man is single at my age, something must be wrong,” he says. “But life just passed. Work, responsibilities, caring for my parents. Then suddenly you look around and you are alone.”

The cleric’s service does not guarantee love. It offers introductions. If both sides agree, families may be informed, meetings arranged and conversations supervised or guided according to the couple’s comfort and religious boundaries.

For Ahmad, even that first step is meaningful.

He says he is not looking for a dramatic romance. He wants companionship: someone to share meals with, to visit relatives with, to discuss ordinary problems with at the end of the day.

“In our culture, marriage is not only two people,” he says. “It is two families, two ways of living. But still, in the home, it is just you and her. That must be peaceful.”

Critics of formal matchmaking say it can feel transactional, reducing intimacy to a checklist. Others argue that family and religious pressure can limit personal choice, especially for women. But supporters say services like this can protect people from unserious relationships and help them speak honestly about expectations before emotions take over.

The cleric says he encourages prospective couples to talk clearly.

“Love is important,” he says. “But marriage also needs patience, responsibility and truth. If people hide things at the beginning, they suffer later.”

Ahmad’s file is placed in a folder with others. Somewhere in the same city, perhaps, another person has answered similar questions and is waiting for a call.

Before leaving, Ahmad straightens his jacket and smiles nervously. He says he knows no system can manufacture affection. But he hopes it can open a door.

“I am not asking for perfection,” he says. “I only want a chance to meet someone who also wants to stay.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a journalistic article about the “matchmaking mullah” of Tehran, including cultural context, applicant fees, meetings, family involvement, counseling services, and colorful quotes from the cleric.
counterfactuals.output:
## Tehran’s “Matchmaking Mullah” Brings Old Traditions to a Modern Marriage Market

**TEHRAN —** In a modest office tucked behind a busy avenue in central Tehran, the walls are lined not with religious texts alone, but with binders: thick, carefully labeled folders containing the hopes of thousands of single Iranians.

Inside them are résumés of a different kind — age, education, profession, family background, religious outlook, expectations for marriage, and sometimes a photograph clipped neatly to the page. At the center of it all sits the cleric many locals know, half-jokingly and half-reverently, as Tehran’s “matchmaking mullah.”

“We are not selling romance,” the cleric says with a smile, adjusting his turban as another family waits outside his door. “We are building bridges. Love may be a flower, but marriage is the garden. Someone must check the soil.”

For years, the cleric’s marriage bureau has offered a culturally familiar answer to a very modern problem: how to find a suitable spouse in a society where young people are more educated, more urban, and more selective than previous generations — yet where family approval, religious values and social reputation still carry enormous weight.

### A modern service with traditional roots

Matchmaking has deep roots in Iranian culture. For generations, marriages were often arranged or introduced through relatives, neighbors, family friends, or trusted community figures. While young Iranians today are far more likely to meet through universities, workplaces, social media or dating apps, many families remain uneasy with completely informal courtship.

That is where the matchmaking cleric steps in.

His office acts as a supervised introduction service, combining elements of old-fashioned family matchmaking with administrative screening and counseling. Applicants fill out detailed forms and are interviewed about their religious practices, finances, education, temperament, health, and expectations for married life.

“I ask them: Do you want a spouse, or do you want a mirror that only praises you?” the cleric says. “Marriage is not a poetry competition. It is patience, bread, respect, and sometimes silence.”

### Fees and files

The service is not free, though it is presented as modest and community-oriented rather than commercial. Applicants typically pay a registration fee to open a file and cover administrative costs. Additional fees may apply for counseling sessions, extended searches or follow-up meetings, depending on the level of service requested.

The cleric insists the fees are intended to keep the office running, not to turn marriage into a business.

“If money could buy a good marriage, the rich would never divorce,” he says. “The fee is for paper, phone calls and time. The blessing is not for sale.”

For many applicants, the fee is also a sign of seriousness. Families say it helps filter out those who are merely curious or unserious about marriage.

### The first meeting: supervised, structured, cautious

Once a possible match is identified, the office contacts both sides discreetly. If the applicants and their families agree, a meeting is arranged — often in the cleric’s office or another respectable setting.

The atmosphere is formal but not cold. Tea is served. Parents may sit nearby. The prospective couple is encouraged to speak, but within boundaries acceptable to their families.

Questions can be direct: Do you plan to work after marriage? Where would you live? How important is religious observance? Would you accept living with in-laws? How many children do you want? What are your views on money, travel, social media, and friendships with the opposite sex?

The cleric says these conversations are essential.

“Some people discuss wedding flowers before they discuss anger,” he says. “Then six months later, they discover the thorns.”

### Families at the center

Unlike many Western dating services, the Tehran matchmaking office places families at the heart of the process. Parents often accompany applicants, review potential matches and help evaluate compatibility. In Iranian society, marriage is widely understood not just as a union between two individuals, but between two families.

That family involvement can be comforting — or complicated.

Some young applicants appreciate having parental support and a trusted intermediary. Others worry that families may dominate the process or place too much emphasis on class, income, ethnicity or appearances.

The cleric says he tries to balance respect for parents with attention to the couple’s wishes.

“A mother’s eyes are useful,” he says, “but they cannot live the marriage for her daughter. A father may ask about salary, but the wife will live with the character.”

### Counseling before and after marriage

Beyond introductions, the office provides counseling — a growing need in a country where marriage is still highly valued but divorce has become more visible, particularly in urban areas.

Premarital counseling sessions cover communication, conflict resolution, sexual expectations, financial planning, religious obligations, family boundaries and legal rights within marriage. Couples may be encouraged to discuss the marriage contract carefully, including conditions that can be added under Iranian law.

The cleric also meets married couples facing difficulties. Some come after arguments over money; others over interference from in-laws, infertility, jealousy, or mismatched expectations.

“People think divorce begins with a shout,” he says. “No. It begins with small disrespect repeated every day.”

His approach mixes religious advice, practical counseling and blunt humor. He urges men to listen more and women not to treat silence as a weapon. He tells couples to avoid comparing their lives to curated images online.

“Instagram has ruined many kitchens,” he jokes. “A man sees another man’s dinner, a woman sees another woman’s flowers, and suddenly both forget the soup in front of them.”

### A response to changing Iran

The popularity of such services reflects wider social shifts in Iran. Young people are marrying later than previous generations, often because of education, unemployment, housing costs and changing aspirations. Many women are highly educated and want both respect and partnership. Many men feel pressure to provide financially in a difficult economy.

At the same time, public dating remains socially sensitive for many families. A cleric-led introduction service offers a culturally acceptable middle path: structured, supervised and religiously legitimate, but more flexible than traditional arranged marriage.

Sociologists say the appeal lies in trust. A cleric with community standing can reassure families that applicants have been screened and that the process is serious.

But critics argue that such services may reinforce conservative expectations, especially around gender roles. They say young people need more freedom to choose partners on their own terms.

The cleric rejects the idea that he is arranging marriages by force.

“I am not a locksmith,” he says. “I do not close doors on people. I open one door and say: Look carefully before entering.”

### Success, failure and fate

Not every introduction leads to marriage. Some applicants reject match after match. Others meet once and never return. A few get engaged quickly, only to reconsider after counseling reveals deep differences.

The cleric says a failed match is not a failure of the process.

“Better a broken proposal than a broken home,” he says.

He keeps track of couples who marry through the office, and some return later with children. Their visits, he says, are his greatest satisfaction.

“When a child comes here and pulls my beard, I say: This is my certificate,” he says, laughing. “Universities give paper. God gives toddlers.”

For all the files, forms and fees, the matchmaking mullah insists his work remains more art than science. Compatibility, he says, cannot be reduced to income, height, education or family name.

“In marriage, two people do not need to be the same,” he says. “If both are drums, there is only noise. One must sometimes be the drum, the other the hand. Together, there is rhythm.”

In a city where tradition and modernity constantly negotiate with one another, his office continues to draw the anxious, the hopeful and the pragmatic — young men and women seeking not just a spouse, but a path through the expectations of family, faith and an uncertain future.

As the afternoon call to prayer echoes faintly beyond the window, another mother enters with a folder in hand. The cleric reaches for his pen.

“Marriage,” he says, “is the only exam where two people must pass together.”
